tools.title: AP Score Release Date 2026
tools.description: Track the 2026 AP score release date, see what to do before scores arrive, and understand how to send AP scores after release.
tools.summary: 2026 AP scores are scheduled to be available starting Monday, July 6, 2026. Use the countdown and quick checklist below to get ready before release day.

tables.caption: AP score release day plan
rows: Before July 6
Make sure you can sign in to your College Board account and recover your password if needed.
Most score-day stress comes from account access problems, not from the scores themselves.
Morning of July 6
Check scores from a private device and avoid repeated rapid refreshes if the site is busy.
Scores can roll out during the day, and heavy traffic can make the official site slower.
After scores appear
Save a private copy for your own records, then check each college's AP credit policy before making schedule decisions.
A score can mean different credit or placement outcomes at different colleges.
If a score is missing
Confirm your exam, account, and school details, then use official College Board support channels.
Missing or delayed scores usually need official account-level help.

tables.caption: After AP scores arrive
rows: Score may earn credit
Look up the exact college, department, and course placement policy.
Do not assume every college treats the same AP score the same way.
Score is lower than expected
Wait before changing plans, then compare options with your school counselor or college advisor.
Do not assume one score determines admission or your whole schedule.
You need to send scores
Use the official score-sending tools and check deadlines.
Do not rely on screenshots as official score reports.
You are still in high school
Use the result to decide future course load and exam planning.
Do not overload next year only because one exam went well.

body.heading: What to know
body.text: AP scores usually roll out through the student's online College Board account. Release timing can vary during the day, so refresh gently and keep your sign-in information ready.

body.heading: Before scores arrive
body.text: Confirm that your College Board account uses the same name and identifying details you used for AP exams. If you are sending scores to a college, review your recipient choices before making changes.

body.heading: How to check your AP scores
body.text: Start from the official AP score page and sign in directly. Avoid links from random messages or social posts on score day. If the site is slow, wait a short while and try again instead of creating a second account.

body.heading: Why a score can be delayed
body.text: A delayed or missing score can happen for account matching, late testing, make-up testing, or processing review. This page cannot access private score data, so any score-specific problem should be handled through official College Board support.

body.heading: Use scores carefully
body.text: AP scores can help with placement and credit, but each college sets its own policy. Before dropping a class, changing a schedule, or sending a report, compare the score with the exact policy for that school and program.

checklist: Confirm your College Board username and password.
Check that your email address and profile details are current.
Write down the colleges or programs that may need your scores.
Avoid sharing screenshots with personal information visible.
Review each college's credit policy before making course decisions.
Keep your AP number or school information handy in case support asks for matching details.
Decide whether you need an official score send or only a personal record.
Make a short list of follow-up questions for your counselor or college advisor.

faq.q: Are all 2026 AP scores released at the exact same minute?
faq.a: No. Scores are scheduled to become available starting July 6, 2026, but individual access can vary during the day.

faq.q: Can this site show my AP score?
faq.a: No. This page is only an unofficial planning tool. Always sign in through the official College Board website to view scores.

faq.q: Should I send scores before seeing them?
faq.a: Many students wait until they understand college credit policies. If a deadline applies, confirm it directly with the college.

faq.q: What should I do if one AP score is missing?
faq.a: Check whether the exam was late-tested or processed separately, then use official College Board support if the score still does not appear.

faq.q: Do colleges automatically receive my AP scores?
faq.a: Not always. Score sending depends on the choices you made and the official score-send process. Check your College Board account and the college's instructions.

faq.q: Can I use a screenshot as proof of my AP score?
faq.a: A screenshot may help you remember your score, but colleges and programs usually require official score reporting for credit or placement.

body.heading: How to use this schedule
body.text: Use this page as a planning overview, then confirm the exact subject-by-subject schedule with your school or the official AP exam calendar.

body.heading: Avoid schedule mistakes
body.text: Students taking multiple AP exams should check for same-day exams, transportation timing, lunch plans, calculator rules, and any school-specific check-in instructions.

body.heading: If two exams feel too close together
body.text: Back-to-back exam days can be tiring even when they do not conflict. Write down travel, meals, sleep, calculator charging, and review time for each exam instead of treating the week as one long study block.

body.heading: Late testing is not a backup plan for convenience
body.text: Late testing is handled through schools and approved situations. If you think you need late testing, contact your AP coordinator early and use official school instructions.

faq.q: Is this the official AP exam calendar?
faq.a: No. This is an unofficial planning page that summarizes key windows. Use College Board and your school for official details.

faq.q: Can my school change my start time?
faq.a: Schools manage local logistics, rooms, and check-in procedures. Confirm exact arrival instructions with your AP coordinator.

faq.q: What if I miss an AP exam?
faq.a: Ask your AP coordinator immediately. Late testing depends on approved reasons and school arrangements.

tools.title: AP Exam Day Checklist
tools.description: A practical AP exam day checklist covering what to bring, what to avoid, and how to prepare the night before.
tools.summary: Use this unofficial AP exam day checklist to pack the basics, reduce morning stress, and avoid preventable testing-day issues.
checklist: Photo ID if your school requires it.
Several No. 2 pencils with erasers.
Black or dark blue pens for written responses if required.
Approved calculator for exams that allow one.
Extra batteries or backup calculator if allowed.
Watch without internet, alarms, or recording features if permitted.
Water and snack for breaks, following school rules.
Layered clothing for cold or warm testing rooms.
Printed or saved room/check-in instructions from your school.
A simple lunch plan if you have morning and afternoon exams on the same day.

tables.caption: AP exam day packing guide
rows: Photo ID
Your school or test site requires identification.
Ask your AP coordinator what ID is accepted.
Calculator
Your exam allows or requires an approved calculator.
Confirm the official calculator policy for that subject.
Pens and pencils
Most written exams require approved writing tools.
Pack extras the night before.
Phone or smartwatch
Only if your school allows storage away from the testing area.
Do not keep devices on your body during testing unless official instructions allow it.
Snack and water
You have a break or a long testing day.
Follow school rules for where food and drinks can be stored.

tables.caption: Night-before and morning timeline
rows: Night before
Pack approved materials and check calculator batteries.
You do not want to troubleshoot during check-in.
Before leaving
Eat something steady and check transportation time.
A rushed morning makes small mistakes more likely.
At school
Follow check-in instructions and store restricted items.
Testing rooms usually have strict device and materials rules.
After the exam
Write down anything you need to ask your teacher or counselor later.
Do not discuss secure exam content online or in public posts.

body.heading: Pack the night before
body.text: Put approved items in one bag and remove anything you do not need. Phones, smartwatches, notes, and unapproved devices can create serious problems in a testing room.

body.heading: Morning routine
body.text: Leave earlier than usual, eat something steady, and arrive with enough time for check-in. If something goes wrong, contact your school immediately instead of guessing.

body.heading: Plan for the room, not the perfect room
body.text: Testing rooms can be cold, warm, quiet, crowded, or farther from your normal classroom than expected. A simple clothing layer, extra pencils, and clear arrival plan solve many avoidable problems.

body.heading: Keep exam security simple
body.text: If an item is not clearly allowed, leave it outside the testing area or ask before check-in. Unapproved notes, devices, and recording tools can create bigger problems than forgetting a snack.

faq.q: Can I bring my phone to an AP exam?
faq.a: Schools usually require phones to be powered off and stored away. Follow your school's instructions and official AP rules.

faq.q: Do I need a calculator for every AP exam?
faq.a: No. Calculator rules depend on the subject. Check the official calculator policy before exam day.

faq.q: Should I bring notes for last-minute review?
faq.a: You can review before check-in if your school allows it, but notes should not enter the testing area unless explicitly permitted.

faq.q: What should I do if I wake up sick on AP exam day?
faq.a: Contact your school or AP coordinator as early as possible. Do not assume you can simply arrive late or choose a later date on your own.

faq.q: Can I leave when I finish early?
faq.a: Testing rooms follow official timing and school procedures. Expect to stay until the proctor releases students.

body.heading: Build a simple SAT plan
body.text: Most students should avoid choosing a test date in isolation. Work backward from application deadlines, school activities, AP exams, travel, and how much practice time you realistically have.

body.heading: Registration reminders
body.text: Registration windows, test center availability, fees, and accommodations deadlines can change. Confirm details in your official College Board account before making plans.

body.heading: Choose a date with a backup plan
body.text: A good SAT plan usually includes one primary date and one possible retake date. That gives you room for illness, technical issues, a lower-than-expected score, or a schedule conflict.

body.heading: Do not ignore school workload
body.text: The best date on paper may be a poor date if it lands beside AP exams, finals, major travel, or a heavy activity season. A slightly later test with better preparation can be smarter than a rushed early test.

faq.q: Are these dates guaranteed?
faq.a: No. They are based on College Board's listed SAT weekend schedule and should be confirmed before registration.

faq.q: How many SAT dates should I plan for?
faq.a: Many students plan one main test date and one backup retake date. Your timeline depends on deadlines and prep progress.

faq.q: Should juniors test in March or May?
faq.a: March gives more retake room. May may fit students who need more prep time, but it can overlap with AP exams.

faq.q: Is August too early for seniors?
faq.a: Not necessarily. August can be useful for seniors who prepared over the summer and want scores before fall deadlines.

faq.q: Should I register before I feel fully ready?
faq.a: A deadline can help your practice plan, but do not choose a date so soon that you cannot complete meaningful review.

faq.q: How should I choose between October and November?
faq.a: Check college deadlines first. October leaves more room for early deadlines, while November may fit regular decision plans for many students.

tools.title: Digital SAT Checklist
tools.description: A digital SAT checklist for devices, Bluebook setup, ID, admission ticket, calculator, and test morning logistics.
tools.summary: The digital SAT depends on both preparation and device readiness. Use this checklist before test day so you are not troubleshooting at the door.
checklist: Install or update Bluebook on your approved device.
Complete exam setup when it becomes available.
Bring an acceptable photo ID.
Bring your admission ticket if required by your test center.
Charge your device fully and bring the power cord.
Bring an approved calculator or use the built-in calculator.
Pack pencils or pens for scratch work if your center provides paper.
Know your test center route, parking, and arrival time.
Restart your device the day before so updates are less likely to interrupt testing.
Turn off unnecessary notifications before arriving at the test center.
Bring a quiet backup plan for transportation if someone else is driving you.

tables.caption: Digital SAT setup timeline
rows: 1-2 weeks before
Install or update Bluebook and confirm your device meets requirements.
Last-minute device problems are harder to solve.
Several days before
Complete exam setup when available and confirm your test center details.
You want login and setup issues solved before test morning.
Night before
Charge your device, pack the charger, ID, admission ticket, and calculator.
A complete bag reduces morning decisions.
Test morning
Arrive early, follow staff instructions, and keep restricted items stored away.
Most test centers run on a strict check-in process.

tables.caption: Digital SAT troubleshooting guide
rows: Bluebook will not open
Restart the device and check whether the app is updated.
Official Bluebook support or test center staff.
Device battery is low
Use your charger before check-in if allowed.
Test center staff for outlet or seating instructions.
You forgot your admission ticket
Check whether you can access or print the required information before check-in.
Test center staff and your College Board account.
Calculator concern
Use an approved calculator or the built-in calculator if allowed for that section.
College Board calculator guidance and test center staff.

body.heading: Device readiness matters
body.text: Do not wait until the morning of the test to open Bluebook. Run through setup, check your operating system, and make sure you know your device password.

body.heading: What not to bring
body.text: Avoid bringing notes, separate timers, recording devices, or other items that could violate test rules. When in doubt, follow College Board and test center instructions.

body.heading: Treat the device like a test material
body.text: Your device is part of the test-day setup, not just a laptop you happen to bring. Keep it charged, updated, and easy to unlock without needing another device.

body.heading: Reduce notification risk
body.text: Before arriving, close unrelated apps and silence avoidable notifications. Follow official instructions for device settings at the test center.

faq.q: Can I take the digital SAT on any laptop?
faq.a: No. Device requirements apply. Check official Bluebook and SAT device guidance before test day.

faq.q: What happens if my device battery dies?
faq.a: Bring your charger and follow test center instructions. A fully charged device is one of the easiest problems to prevent.

faq.q: Is this checklist official?
faq.a: No. It is an unofficial planning checklist that points you back to official SAT rules.

faq.q: Should I update my operating system right before the SAT?
faq.a: Avoid unnecessary last-minute changes. Check official device guidance, and complete updates early enough to test Bluebook afterward.

faq.q: Do I need a separate calculator?
faq.a: Some students bring an approved calculator even when a built-in calculator is available. Check official calculator rules and bring only allowed devices.

tools.title: SAT Score Release Guide
tools.description: Understand how SAT score release usually works, what to check before scores arrive, and how to think about sending scores.
tools.summary: SAT score release timing depends on the administration. This unofficial guide helps you prepare your account, college list, and next-step decisions before scores post.

body.heading: Where scores appear
body.text: SAT scores appear in the student's College Board account after processing. Some scores may take longer if additional review or matching is needed.

body.heading: After scores post
body.text: Compare your score with college testing policies, scholarship requirements, and your own retake plan. If you send scores, use official College Board score sending tools.

body.heading: Read the score before reacting
body.text: Look at the total score, section scores, and your original goal. A score that feels disappointing may still be useful for some colleges, scholarships, or a superscore strategy.

body.heading: Use deadlines to decide on sending
body.text: Before sending any score, check each college's current testing policy, deadline, and score choice rules. Some colleges accept self-reported scores at first, while others require official reports.

body.heading: Plan retakes with evidence
body.text: A retake is most useful when you know what you will change. Use your score report and practice history to pick a focused improvement plan instead of simply registering again.

checklist: Confirm your College Board sign-in works.
Save your test date and registration details.
Make a short list of colleges that may need official scores.
Check each college's test policy and deadline.
Decide whether a retake date still fits your timeline.
Compare your score with each college's published middle-range or testing policy if available.
Check whether a college uses superscoring or score choice.
Make a small retake plan before registering again.

tables.caption: SAT score release next steps
rows: Score meets your target
Check college reporting rules and decide whether official sending is needed.
Sending scores blindly without checking each policy.
One section is weaker
Plan focused practice for that section before a retake.
Repeating the same broad study routine.
Score is delayed
Check your account and official support guidance.
Creating another account or relying on unofficial score rumors.
Deadline is close
Confirm whether the college accepts that test date and when scores must arrive.
Assuming every school has the same deadline.
You may superscore
Check whether each college combines section scores from different dates.
Assuming superscoring is universal.

tables.caption: Retake decision guide
rows: Do you have at least several weeks to improve?
Choose a retake date with a focused plan.
Retaking immediately may not change much.
Did one section hold back your total?
Target that section first.
A full review plan may be better.
Will colleges accept the later score?
Register if the timeline works.
Do not spend money on a score that arrives too late.
Can you manage the workload?
Build practice into your weekly schedule.
Protect grades, applications, and sleep first.

faq.q: Does TestDayTools know my SAT score release time?
faq.a: No. This is an unofficial guide. Use your College Board account for actual scores and official updates.

faq.q: Why are some SAT scores delayed?
faq.a: Scores can be delayed for matching issues, make-up testing, or additional review. Contact College Board for official help.

faq.q: Should I send all SAT scores?
faq.a: Policies vary by college. Check whether each college accepts score choice, superscores, or requires all scores.

faq.q: Should I retake the SAT if my score improved only a little?
faq.a: Maybe. Compare the score with your college list, deadlines, practice time, and whether one section has clear room for improvement.

faq.q: What is superscoring?
faq.a: Superscoring means a college may combine your best section scores from different test dates. Policies vary, so check each college.

body.heading: How to study
body.text: Start with the official California Driver Handbook, then use practice questions to check whether you can apply the rules in plain language.

body.heading: What this quiz covers
body.text: The questions focus on general safe-driving knowledge: right of way, signs, lane use, alcohol rules, speed, and defensive driving.

faq.q: Are these official California DMV questions?
faq.a: No. They are original practice questions made for study. Always use the California DMV handbook for official rules.

faq.q: Can this quiz guarantee I pass?
faq.a: No. It is a practice aid, not a guarantee. Read the handbook and follow official DMV instructions.

faq.q: Does this page collect my answers?
faq.a: No. The quiz runs in your browser and does not collect personal information.

tools.title: New York DMV Permit Practice Test
tools.description: Practice original New York permit-style questions about traffic signs, road rules, alcohol, intersections, and safe driving.
tools.summary: Use these original, unofficial New York permit practice questions to review common road rules before studying the official manual again.

body.heading: Study flow
body.text: Read the official New York driver's manual first, then use practice questions to catch weak spots. Revisit the manual after each missed question.

body.heading: Question style
body.text: These questions are written in a general permit-test style and cover safe choices drivers should understand before driving alone.

faq.q: Are these real New York DMV test questions?
faq.a: No. These are original practice questions and are not copied from the official exam.

faq.q: Is this affiliated with the New York DMV?
faq.a: No. TestDayTools is independent and unofficial.

faq.q: Where should I verify a rule?
faq.a: Use the official New York driver's manual or contact the DMV for official guidance.

california.q: When approaching a stop sign, what should you do?
choices: Come to a complete stop before the limit line or crosswalk
Slow down only if another car is present
Stop after entering the intersection
california.explanation: A complete stop before the limit line or crosswalk gives drivers and pedestrians predictable space.

california.q: If a traffic signal is not working, you should usually treat the intersection as:
choices: A green light for the larger road
A four-way stop
A yield sign for every driver
california.explanation: When signals fail, drivers should use stop-sign style caution unless directed otherwise by an officer or posted control.

california.q: A solid yellow line on your side of the road generally means:
choices: Passing is not allowed from your lane
You may pass whenever the road is clear
The lane is reserved for buses
california.explanation: A solid yellow line indicates passing restrictions for traffic on that side.

california.q: What is the safest response when an emergency vehicle approaches with lights and siren?
choices: Pull to the right and stop when safe
Speed up to stay ahead of it
Stop immediately in your lane without checking traffic
california.explanation: Drivers should yield by moving right and stopping when it can be done safely.

choices: Signal, check mirrors, and look over your shoulder
Signal only after moving
Rely only on the rearview mirror
california.explanation: Mirrors do not cover every blind spot, so a shoulder check is important.

california.q: When driving in fog, which choice is usually safest?
choices: Use low-beam headlights and slow down
Use high beams so you can see farther
Drive close to the vehicle ahead
california.explanation: Low beams reduce glare in fog, and slower speed gives you more time to react.

california.q: A pedestrian is crossing at an unmarked crosswalk at an intersection. You should:
choices: Yield and let the pedestrian cross safely
Honk so the pedestrian stops
Drive through if you are below the speed limit
california.explanation: Drivers should yield to pedestrians crossing legally at intersections and marked crosswalks.

california.q: What does a red curb usually mean?
choices: Loading zone for passengers only
Parking allowed for a short time
No stopping, standing, or parking
california.explanation: Red curb rules generally prohibit stopping, standing, or parking except where official signs say otherwise.

california.q: If your vehicle begins to hydroplane, what should you do first?
choices: Ease off the accelerator and steer straight
Brake hard immediately
Turn sharply toward the shoulder
california.explanation: Sudden braking or sharp steering can make a skid worse. Ease off and keep the vehicle pointed where you want to go.

california.q: At night, you should dim high beams when approaching another vehicle because:
choices: High beams use too much battery power
Bright lights can blind other drivers
It makes your car easier to hear
california.explanation: High beams can create glare for oncoming drivers and drivers ahead of you.

california.q: If a school bus ahead has flashing red lights, the safest general response is to:
choices: Stop as required and watch for children
Pass quickly before children step out
Move into the left lane and keep driving
california.explanation: Flashing red school bus lights mean children may be entering or leaving the roadway.

california.q: Which choice best describes defensive driving?
choices: Expecting hazards and leaving yourself time to react
Driving faster than traffic to avoid clusters
Using the horn whenever traffic slows
california.explanation: Defensive driving means scanning ahead, keeping space, and preparing for mistakes by other road users.

california.q: When parking uphill with a curb, your front wheels should generally be turned:
choices: Toward the curb
Straight ahead only
Away from the curb
california.explanation: Turning wheels away from the curb helps the curb stop the vehicle if it rolls backward.

california.q: What should you do if another driver is tailgating you?
choices: Increase your following distance from the car ahead and let the tailgater pass when safe
Tap your brakes repeatedly
Speed up until the tailgater disappears
california.explanation: Creating more room ahead gives you a gentler braking cushion and can reduce pressure behind you.

california.q: Before entering a roundabout, you should:
choices: Yield to traffic already in the roundabout
Stop inside the roundabout to check signs
Enter quickly because entering traffic has priority
california.explanation: Drivers entering a roundabout generally yield to vehicles already circulating.

newyork.q: At a flashing red traffic light, a driver should:
choices: Stop completely, then proceed when safe
Continue if no police officer is present
Treat it like a green light
newyork.explanation: A flashing red light works like a stop sign: stop, yield, then proceed safely.

newyork.q: When two vehicles arrive at a four-way stop at the same time, which driver generally has the right of way?
choices: The driver turning left
The driver on the right
The driver with the larger vehicle
newyork.explanation: At a same-time arrival, the driver on the right generally goes first.

newyork.q: What should you do when following a motorcycle?
choices: Leave extra following distance
Follow closely so cars cannot cut in
Use high beams during the day
newyork.explanation: Motorcycles can stop quickly and are affected by road conditions, so extra space helps.

newyork.q: A yellow diamond-shaped sign usually means:
choices: Service area ahead
Parking regulation
Warning or caution
newyork.explanation: Yellow diamond signs warn drivers about road conditions or hazards ahead.

newyork.q: If you miss your highway exit, the safest choice is to:
choices: Continue to the next exit
Back up on the shoulder
Make a sudden lane change across traffic
newyork.explanation: Continue to the next safe exit. Backing up or swerving is dangerous and illegal in many situations.

newyork.q: A steady yellow traffic light usually means:
choices: The light is about to turn red
Traffic may speed through the intersection
Only buses must stop
newyork.explanation: A steady yellow light warns that the signal is changing to red, so drivers should stop if they can do so safely.

newyork.q: Before backing out of a driveway, you should:
choices: Rely only on the backup camera
Check behind, move slowly, and watch for pedestrians
Back quickly to reduce time in the roadway
newyork.explanation: Cameras and mirrors help, but drivers should still check carefully and move slowly.

newyork.q: What does a white rectangular regulatory sign usually tell drivers?
choices: A law or rule that must be followed
A scenic route nearby
A warning about a curve
newyork.explanation: Regulatory signs commonly use white backgrounds and explain traffic laws or required actions.

newyork.q: If an oncoming vehicle crosses into your lane, you should generally:
choices: Slow down, move right if possible, and avoid a head-on crash
Swerve left into oncoming traffic
Flash your lights and keep your speed
newyork.explanation: Reducing speed and moving right when safe can create more escape space.

newyork.q: When roads are wet, you should increase following distance because:
choices: Stopping takes longer
Speed limits no longer apply
Brakes work instantly on wet roads
newyork.explanation: Wet pavement reduces tire grip and increases stopping distance.

choices: Only the space directly behind your trunk
A lane reserved for emergency vehicles
An area around your vehicle that mirrors may not show
newyork.explanation: Blind spots are areas not fully visible in mirrors, so checking over your shoulder matters.

newyork.q: If you see a bicyclist ahead, the best approach is to:
choices: Leave safe passing space and watch for sudden movement
Honk continuously until they move
Pass closely to stay in your lane
newyork.explanation: Bicyclists may need to avoid debris or road hazards, so extra space is important.

newyork.q: When approaching railroad tracks with flashing signals, you should:
choices: Stop before the tracks and wait until it is safe
Drive around the gate if no train is visible
Stop on the tracks for a better view
newyork.explanation: Never drive around lowered gates or stop on tracks. Wait until signals clear and the crossing is safe.

newyork.q: If you are tired while driving, the safest choice is to:
choices: Pull over safely and rest
Open a window and keep driving no matter what
Follow another vehicle closely to stay alert
newyork.explanation: Drowsy driving slows reaction time. Resting is safer than trying to push through fatigue.

newyork.q: At an intersection with a yield sign, you should:
choices: Slow down and give right of way to traffic or pedestrians already in the intersection
Stop only if a police officer is present
Accelerate so other drivers can merge behind you
newyork.explanation: A yield sign requires drivers to slow and let conflicting traffic or pedestrians proceed before entering.

trustPages.title: About TestDayTools
trustPages.description: Learn what TestDayTools is, how the site is maintained, and why all tools are unofficial.

content.heading: What we make
content.text: TestDayTools is a small, independent website that turns test logistics into quick tools: dates, checklists, score guides, and practice pages.

content.heading: How we work
content.text: Pages are built from simple data files so dates, FAQs, checklists, and practice questions can be updated without redesigning the site.

content.heading: Affiliation
content.text: We are not affiliated with College Board, AP, SAT, any DMV, or any government agency. Names are used only to describe the exams and public services students are researching.

trustPages.title: Privacy Policy
trustPages.description: Privacy policy for TestDayTools. The MVP does not collect personal information or store quiz answers.

content.heading: Personal information
content.text: This MVP does not ask for names, emails, account numbers, scores, driver's license numbers, or other personal information.

content.heading: Quiz answers
content.text: Practice quiz answers are checked in your browser. They are not submitted to a server by this static site.

content.heading: Future ads and analytics
content.text: The site may later use privacy-conscious analytics or advertising services. If that happens, this policy should be updated before launch.

trustPages.title: Contact
trustPages.description: Contact information and correction requests for TestDayTools.

content.heading: Corrections
content.text: If you find an outdated date, broken source link, or unclear explanation, use the public project page at github.com/carmenjiang19028-ai/testdaytools until a dedicated domain email is connected.

content.heading: No official support
content.text: For official AP, SAT, score, registration, permit, or license questions, contact College Board or the relevant DMV directly.

trustPages.title: Disclaimer

content.heading: Unofficial site
content.text: TestDayTools is fan-made and unofficial. It is not affiliated with College Board, AP, SAT, any DMV, or any government agency.

content.heading: No guarantees
content.text: Dates, policies, and rules can change. Use official sources for final decisions about exam registration, score sending, credit, permits, and licensing.
